name: Santiago Mitlatongo Mixtec
confidence_why: No description of Mitlatongo Mixtec stress has been found: McKendry 2001, Whitman 2006 and Hollenbach 2017 say nothing about it, and the only pointer is Josserand 1983's family-wide claim, known here only through Carroll 2015, that every Mixtec couplet carries stress on its first syllable.

PhD dissertation, University of California, San Diego (eScholarship qt0bs6b7mt), sec. 4.2.1 'Default stress', p. 86, quoting Josserand, J. Kathryn. 1983. Mixtec Dialect History. PhD dissertation, Tulane University, p. 180 (primary unreachable: ProQuest/UMI only; archive.org, Google Books API/feed and HathiTrust full-text search all negative or blocked in Stages A-C). First-hand Mitlatongo sources opened, none of which discusses stress: McKendry, Inga. 2001. Two studies of Mixtec languages. MA thesis, University of North Dakota (Paper 1, thesis pp. 20-30); Whitman, LeRoy J. 2006. Alfabeto del mixteco de Mitlatongo. Mexico: ILV (4 pp., picture alphabet); Hollenbach, Barbara E. 2017. Notes on Mixtec terms for supernatural beings. SIL Mexico (lexical survey).
catalog_locator: Carroll 2015 sec. 4.2 'Survey of stress descriptions in Mixtec varieties', subsec. 4.2.1 'Default stress' (heading p. 84, as in the table of contents); quoted passage p. 86; domain sentence (K. L. Pike 1948 couplet) p. 85; Yoloxochitl counterexample in subsec. 4.2.2 'Final stress', p. 87; Table A.2 p. 276 (row 'Santiago Mitlatongo Mit Mitl vmm Alta:NE'). page numbers sit in the running head at the top of each page. Josserand 1983:180 as cited there. McKendry 2001: Mitlatongo (SM) passages in Paper 1, pp. 20-30; its stress remarks occur only at pp. 42, 53, 70, 131 (Paper 2, Southeastern Nochixtlan Mixtec [mxy], and its appendix).
catalog_quote: Generalizing across Mixtec varieties, Josserand (1983:180) defines the couplet as “composed of two syllables and carrying stress on the first of these two,” implying that all Mixtec varieties have the same stress behavior. Besides the data from Santo Domingo Nuxaa shown in (4.2), several other descriptions support the characterization of stress in Mixtec as falling on the first vowel of the couplet. ... In sum, default stress on the first syllable of the couplet is widely reported in Mixtec.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: verified against the full PDF (362 pp; extracted text). p. 108 carries printed page number 86 and reads exactly: 'Generalizing across Mixtec varieties, Josserand (1983:180) defines the couplet as "composed of two syllables and carrying stress on the first of these two," implying that all Mixtec varieties have the same stress behavior.' The saved excerpt (mitl1235/) matches the PDF line for line. Table A.2 at p. 298 (printed 276) has the row 'Santiago Mitlatongo / Mit / Mitl / vmm / Alta:NE'; the abbreviation 'Mit' occurs nowhere else in Carroll's text (a full-text search for stress/accent), so Carroll uses no Mitlatongo data. Penner 2019 (printed p. 91) independently cites 'Josserand…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level generalization only: stress falls on the first syllable of the disyllabic (bimoraic) root couplet; prefixes and clitics are outside the couplet and unstressed (the latter stated by McKendry 2001 for Southeastern Nochixtlán Mixtec, not for Mitlatongo). No Mitlatongo-specific stress description exists in any source opened.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned for Mitlatongo in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Mitlatongo. Carroll (pp. 86-93) notes that some varieties (e.g. Ayutla, Molinos, Mixtepec per Pike & Ibach 1978) show tone-dependent stress or couplet-initial lengthening rather than a plain initial-stress rule; nothing is reported for Mitlatongo.
new_statements.domain_note: Couplet = the bimoraic/disyllabic root that forms the nucleus of the Mixtec word; the claim is about stress on the first syllable of that root, made by Josserand (1983:180) as a generalization over all varieties in her dialect survey (which includes Santiago Mitlatongo, Josserand code 'Mitl', Carroll Table A.2 p. 276). It is not a Mitlatongo-specific observation; the only first-hand Mitlatongo description opened (McKendry 2001, Paper 1) is silent on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog mitl1235 = ISO vmm, Santiago Mitlatongo and Santa Cruz Mitlatongo (INALI variant "tu'un lavi <mixteco de Mitlatongo>"). Not to be confused with Yutanduchi Mixtec [mab, yuta1240], which Wikipedia pairs with it (c. 70% intelligibility), nor with Southeastern Nochixtlán Mixtec [mxy, sout3002], the Santo Domingo Nuxaá variety that McKendry's 2001 sketch and 2013 PhD describe and for which a first-hand root-initial stress statement exists. ELP lumps vmm into 'Eastern Alta Mixtec' (10529). Josserand's survey code for Mitlatongo is 'Mitl' (Carroll 2015 Table A.2), dialect area Alta:NE.

sources.citation: McKendry, Inga. 2001. Two studies of Mixtec languages. MA thesis, University of North Dakota (UND Theses and Dissertations 4484), vi+131 pp. Paper 1 = 'The phonology of nasalization and palatalization in Mixtec' (thesis pp. 9-39); Paper 2 = typological grammar sketch of Southeastern Nochixtlán Mixtec [mxy].
sources.note: Nothing for Mitlatongo. Paper 1 uses Santiago Mitlatongo (SM) data from McKendry's own field notes plus SIL colleague Leroy Whitman (App. 2, thesis pp. 126-127 = PDF 127-128) for segmental/nasalization facts only (thesis pp. 20-30 = PDF 21-31: Proto-Mixtec *s > /l/, [l] barred before nasal vowels, *k > [x] in nasal morphemes, [-continuant] medial consonants block nasal spread). The only stress remarks (thesis pp. 41, 52, 69, 130 = PDF 42, 53, 70, 131: clitics and prefixes 'unstressed'; '/y/ is realised as [ʒ] in stressed syllables and [j] in unstressed syllables') belong to Paper 2 on Southea…
